title: The coat (Genesis 37:1–11)
hookLine: a favorite son, a special coat, and dreams of sheaves bowing down

lines: THE BIGGER PHOTO ON THE FRIDGE.
cards: The later curfew. The bigger photo on the fridge. In some homes, a favorite child is the thing nobody says out loud.

In Jacob's house, nobody even pretends. Joseph is seventeen, Rachel's son, and Rachel is gone. He tends the flocks with his older brothers and brings back bad reports about some of them to their father.
Then one day Jacob gives Joseph a gift. Only Joseph. Something the brothers see every single day.

teach.b: The Torah says it straight out: "Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age; and he made him a coat of many colours."
Many colors is how the old translations put it, and the musical too.
But nobody is sure what the Hebrew means. The words are ketonet passim. Ketonet is a tunic.
Passim is the puzzle. Many colors is one old guess. Others think it means long sleeves, reaching to the palms and the ankles: a coat for someone who doesn't have to work in the fields.

The phrase turns up again in the book of Samuel, worn by a king's daughter. Whatever it looked like, the brothers understood it perfectly. They hated him, the text says, and couldn't speak a peaceful word to him.
Then Joseph has dreams, and tells them.

teach.h: SHEAVES, SUN, MOON AND STARS BOW.
teach.b: Sheaves of grain in a field, and all the brothers' sheaves bow down to his. Then the sun, the moon and eleven stars bow down to him.
Even Jacob scolds him for that one, but the text says his father kept the saying in mind. The Talmud draws a lesson from the coat.

teach.h: A LITTLE WOOL, AND DOWN TO EGYPT.
teach.b: Never favor one child over the others, it says: for a little bit of fine wool that Jacob gave Joseph beyond his brothers, they grew jealous, and in the end our ancestors went down into Egypt.
The whole story of slavery in Egypt, the Talmud says, begins with a coat.

how: The Joseph story is read in synagogue over several weekly portions in the winter, and the Talmud's lesson from the coat (Shabbat 10b) is a classic text on treating children evenly.

o: a shepherd's cloak for cold nights outside
a gift that marked Joseph as the favorite
a banner the brothers carried into battle

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: the puzzle: colors, or long sleeves?
a little wool, and down to Egypt

s: the Hebrew clearly says the coat had many colors
ketonet passim is uncertain. many colors is one old guess; long sleeves is another.
Joseph was seventeen when the story begins
the text gives his age, and says he tended the flocks with his brothers.
he scolded him, but the text says he kept the saying in mind.

games.q: you're Joseph. you've dreamed that your brothers' sheaves bowed down to yours. they already can't stand you. what do you do?
games.why: he tells them, and then tells them a second dream. the text says they hated him yet the more.

practice: Think of a place in your life where someone gets a little more: more attention, more patience, more credit. Maybe you're the one who gets it, maybe you watch someone else get it; notice what it does to the people around it.
You don't have to fix anything, just see it clearly, the way the brothers saw that coat every day.

wordCard.voice: The coat. Ketonet passim, a gift for the favorite son. Nobody's sure what it looked like, but everyone knew what it meant.

orig.note: Hebrew: Joseph's coat. ketonet is a tunic; the meaning of passim is uncertain.

carryVoice: Your line: favorites cost. For Jacob's family, a little fine wool cost a great deal. Sixty-five days in.

sources.q: Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age; and he made him a coat of many colours.
